practice.title: One Vow, One Week
agreedSteps: Choose one of the eight precepts of aspiring bodhichitta and really go wild on it for the whole week.
Work on incremental steps to develop the four characteristics of a Buddha — grow your skill, impartiality, compassion without discrimination, and freedom from obstructions.
steps: The eight precepts to choose from: (1) remember the benefits of bodhichitta six times a day, (2) generate bodhichitta six times a day, (3) not abandon any living being, (4) accumulate merit and wisdom, (5) not cheat or deceive our Preceptors or Spiritual Guide, (6) not criticize those who have entered the Mahayana, (7) not cause others to regret their virtuous actions, (8) not pretend to have good qualities or hide our faults without a special, pure intention.

Memorize the four characteristics of a Buddha: (1) freedom from all obstructions preventing liberation and omniscience, (2) great skill in liberating living beings from their suffering, (3) compassion for all living beings without discrimination, (4) benefiting all living beings whether or not they've helped us.
With each characteristic, contemplate why you personally want it — not because Buddha said so, but because you understand the pain and limitation of not having it.
Practice the Manjushri DHI recitation to develop quick wisdom — mentally recite DHI rapidly on the breath, imagining orange light blessings from Manjushri entering and mixing with your heart.
practice.quote: It'd be nice for us each — maybe we can all choose one that speaks to us. [It could be] the six-times-a-day ones, or whatever, and then really go wild on it for the week.

commentary.title: Staying in the Game
content: The results of actions increase. All the good karma we make keeps growing and increasing like crazy. But we have to stay in the game and give it enough space to increase. It's like those famous investors who say their secret is that they're not smart — they just stayed in the game. They put some money in some fund 50 years ago and decided not to move it. Everyone else kept moving theirs. And now they have $100 billion, and everyone else is broke.

Our karma growing is an exponential curve, not a linear one. It whips up vertically. So even though it feels like a big deal — 'I'm going to become a Buddha for the benefit of all, whoa' — we don't want to extrapolate linearly. We just have to give it a little time.
commentary.quote: No one else is going to save the living beings of samsara. It's my job.

commentary.title: The Four Characteristics of a Buddha
content: When we contemplate the four characteristics of an awakened being — freedom from all obstructions, great skill, compassion without discrimination, and benefiting all regardless of whether they've helped us — these are what turn us from simply being compassionate into a bodhisattva. It's specifically by thinking about these that we generate the thought, 'I need to become a Buddha for the benefit of all.'

These are non-negotiable memorization items. They should be hard-wired into us like our childhood telephone number. We want to get a feeling of really wanting each one — not because Buddha said so, but because we personally understand the pain and limitation of not having them.

For example, benefiting all living beings whether or not they've helped us — think how petty and miserable it is to only help the people who help us. We're like a mobster doing favors. We don't want to live like that. Or compassion without discrimination — it's trying to find all the people we've scorned, neglected, or don't even think about, and seeing how limiting that is. Great skill — just seeing how powerless we are, how often we've tried to help and made things worse.

commentary.title: Moving the Four Characteristics Forward
content: To get the qualities of a Buddha, we don't just sit there with nothing and then one day — boop! — we're a Buddha with all these skills. We become a Buddha by working on these four skills today. It's a spectrum. We start creating the grooves in our mind.

Great skill, for example: how do you get it? You fail. You practice trying to help people and repeatedly fail over and over. You overdo it, underdo it, get too wrathful sometimes, too gentle other times, and you start to learn. You can't get more skillful on the sidelines.

Part of great skill is understanding the diversity of people and not treating everyone as a two-dimensional object. Most of us project what we are and what we like onto everyone else — which is completely wrong. We can contemplate Dorje Shugden's four compatriots, who represent pacifying, increasing, controlling, and wrathful actions. Do we know the situations where each is appropriate? Are we even discriminating like that, or just winging it?

commentary.title: Quick Wisdom Through Manjushri
content: One of the easiest ways to increase our skill is to increase our quick wisdom through relying on Buddha Manjushri. On a breath, we mentally recite DHI DHI DHI DHI rapidly, imagining blessings from Manjushri in the form of orange light pouring into the syllable DHI. We swallow it, and it mixes with our heart and mind, giving us quick wisdom.

Quick wisdom is what helps us make a decisive, right choice in a moment. Often we need to call on skill in situations that involve a pretty much instantaneous action and response. Manjushri's blessings can help us do this.

commentary.title: The Eight Precepts of Aspiring Bodhichitta
content: The first four precepts prevent the aspiring mind from degenerating in this life: (1) remember the benefits of bodhichitta six times a day, (2) generate bodhichitta six times a day, (3) not abandon any living being, (4) accumulate merit and wisdom.

The last four prevent the aspiring mind from degenerating in future lives: (5) not cheat or deceive our Preceptors or Spiritual Guide, (6) not criticize those who have entered the Mahayana, (7) not cause others to regret their virtuous actions, (8) not pretend to have good qualities or hide our faults without a special, pure intention.

This last one is just about not being pretentious or having concealment. It doesn't mean shouting our inadequacies from the rooftops — that's often its own coping mechanism, a performative insecurity. The point is simply not projecting something that's not true, nor actively suppressing something that is true.

commentary.title: Vows Are Practices, Not Rules
content: When we probe any Dharma question, we always want to ask: how is what I'm looking at a practice? These eight precepts are not just rules. They're practices — invitations.

Not cheating or deceiving our spiritual guide, for example, is a practice of keeping an open conversation going with our spiritual guide throughout the day. It's like keeping an ongoing group chat open with your best friend. Never closing it off. Never hiding ourselves — even in our worst day, in our lowest state.

The bodhisattva vow is made of clay, not glass. When we break a vow, it's not like glass shattering — irreparable harm. It's like clay, and we try again. The principal vow is the intention to keep it. That's level one. Keeping it flawlessly is level two — that's aspirational. If we haven't given up the intention, we haven't actually broken the vow.

If we abandon the intention completely — that is officially a bit like turning on our spiritual guide. But even in our worst moments, we can keep the conduit open: 'I'm a mess today. I got nothing. But I love you, my guru, and I know you love me, and you'll be with me on the other side of this.'
commentary.quote: Not cheating or deceiving our spiritual guide — that's a practice. A practice of keeping an open conversation going, an honest connection going throughout the day. That's what we're being invited to do.

Not cheating or deceiving our spiritual guide, that's a practice. It's a practice of keeping an open conversation going, an honest connection going throughout the day. That's the practice. That's what we're being invited to do.

commentary.title: Bodhichitta as Decision, Not Aspiration
content: There's a difference between a determination and a decision. A decision is: I am going to do this. Not 'I'm aspiring to,' but 'I am going to.' That's the mind we want to get to with respect to becoming a Buddha for the benefit of all.

In the bodhisattva vow, we make a promise to become enlightened for the benefit of all. Are we treating it as a real decision, a real promise? Or are we treating it as an aspirational 'let's go for lunch sometime' — something we say to be polite? Our mind has the capacity to make it a real decision. It's incredibly powerful.
commentary.quote: Am I treating my bodhisattva vow as a decision, as a real promise? Or am I treating it as an aspirational 'let's go for lunch sometime' kind of thing?

commentary.title: Finding a Living Spiritual Guide
content: If we choose Buddha Shakyamuni or Je Tsongkhapa as our spiritual guide, that means they're Buddhas. And if they're Buddhas, they have to have human emanations appearing in our world. If they don't, they're not Buddhas. So it's on us — we need to find where those emanations are, so we can have a chat with them and be guided directly.

We can't have a full-blown conversation with Buddha's enjoyment body or truth body unless we've attained tranquil abiding. If we say 'something is speaking to me,' that could just be a spirit — we have no idea. So we need a living human representation of the Buddhas who can guide us directly.

Part of the practice of reliance on a spiritual guide is learning to see purity in the world. The human we choose as our spiritual guide is the first person we get really good at seeing beyond the ordinary with. That person becomes a paradigm we then apply to all other living beings — including ourselves. If we can't see purity in at least one person, we'll never see it in ourselves or anyone else.
